title: Inheritance
summary: How alleles are passed from parents to offspring through gametes, and how dominance, multiple alleles, sex linkage and polygenes shape phenotypes.

keyterms.definition: The combination of alleles of a gene (or genes) carried by an organism.
The observable traits of an organism, resulting from its genotype and interaction with the environment.
Having two identical alleles of a gene.
Having two different alleles of a gene.
An allele that has the same effect on the phenotype whether homozygous or heterozygous.
An allele that only affects the phenotype when homozygous, because a dominant allele masks it.
Both alleles in a heterozygote are fully expressed in the phenotype, e.g. blood group AB.
The heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype, e.g. pink flowers from red and white alleles.
A gene with more than two alleles in the gene pool, e.g. the ABO blood group gene with IA, IB and i.
Capacity of an organism to develop traits suited to its environment by changing gene expression, without changing its genotype.
A gene located on a sex chromosome (usually the X), so its inheritance pattern differs between males and females.
A characteristic controlled by many genes, each with a small additive effect, producing continuous variation.
Random orientation of homologous pairs in meiosis I, so alleles of unlinked genes pass into gametes independently.
Genes on the same autosome tend to be inherited together because they are not separated by independent assortment.
Offspring or chromosome with a new combination of linked alleles, produced by crossing over in prophase I.
Statistical test comparing observed with expected frequencies to decide whether differences are significant.

questions.prompt: What is the basis of inheritance in sexual reproduction?
options: Fusion of two diploid cells from each parent
Haploid gametes, each with one allele of each gene, fuse to form a diploid zygote
The zygote receives all its alleles from the mother
Gametes are produced by mitosis and fuse to form a haploid zygote
questions.explanation: Meiosis in each parent produces haploid gametes carrying one allele of each gene. Fertilization combines them, so the diploid zygote has two alleles of each gene, one from each parent.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

pairs.right: Combination of alleles an organism has
Two identical alleles of a gene
Two different alleles of a gene

questions.explanation: Genotype is the alleles present; phenotype is what is expressed, influenced by both genotype and environment.

questions.statement: A recessive allele has no effect on the phenotype of a heterozygous individual.
questions.explanation: In a heterozygote the dominant allele determines the phenotype. Often the recessive allele codes for a non-functional protein, and one functional allele gives enough product.

questions.text: Two heterozygous parents (Aa x Aa) are expected to produce offspring with a ___ ratio of dominant to recessive phenotypes.
questions.explanation: The genotypes AA, Aa, aA, aa occur in a 1:2:1 ratio; AA and Aa both show the dominant phenotype, giving 3:1.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of phenotypic plasticity?
options: A mutation giving a plant red flowers
A plant growing larger, thinner leaves in shade than in full sun
Inheriting blood group AB
A heterozygote showing the dominant phenotype
questions.explanation: The same genotype develops different traits in different environments by changing gene expression. The genotype itself does not change, so the trait is not passed on as such.

questions.prompt: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is caused by a recessive allele. What is its effect?
options: Excess tyrosine is made, damaging the liver
Red blood cells become sickle-shaped
Blood fails to clot due to lack of factor VIII
The enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine is not made, so phenylalanine accumulates
questions.explanation: PKU homozygotes lack functional phenylalanine hydroxylase. Phenylalanine builds up and can damage brain development; it is managed by a low-phenylalanine diet after newborn screening.

questions.statement: Two parents without PKU can have a child with PKU.
questions.explanation: If both parents are heterozygous carriers, each child has a 1 in 4 chance of inheriting two recessive alleles.

questions.text: A single base difference in a DNA sequence between individuals is called a single-nucleotide ___.
questions.explanation: SNPs are positions where the base varies within a population. They are the usual way new alleles differ, producing multiple alleles in a gene pool.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for performing a genetic cross between two pure-breeding plant varieties.
items: Remove anthers from the flowers of the female parent before they mature
Transfer pollen from the male parent to the stigma
Cover the flower with a bag to prevent other pollination
Collect and sow seeds to grow the F1 generation
Cross F1 plants to produce the F2 generation
questions.explanation: Emasculation and bagging ensure only the chosen pollen fertilizes the ovules. F1 offspring are then crossed to reveal ratios in the F2.

questions.prompt: Which statement about phenotype is correct?
options: Phenotype is determined only by genotype
Phenotype results from both genotype and environment
Phenotype includes only visible features, not biochemical ones
Changes in phenotype during life are always inherited
questions.explanation: Phenotype includes all observable characteristics (including biochemical ones such as blood group) and depends on genotype and environment. Acquired changes are not inherited.

lessons.title: Multiple alleles, sex linkage and continuous variation

questions.prompt: A person with blood group A (IA i) and a person with blood group B (IB i) have children. Which blood groups are possible?
options: A and B only
AB only
A, B, AB and O
A, B and AB only
questions.explanation: Gametes IA or i combine with IB or i, giving IAIB (AB), IAi (A), IBi (B) and ii (O) in equal proportions.

questions.prompt: Match each ABO genotype to its blood group.
questions.explanation: IA and IB are codominant; both are dominant to i, so group O is only seen in ii homozygotes.

questions.text: Red-flowered and white-flowered four o'clock plants produce pink offspring. This is an example of ___.
questions.explanation: The heterozygote is intermediate between the two homozygotes. In codominance both alleles show fully, as in blood group AB.

questions.statement: In humans, sex is determined by the SRY gene on the Y chromosome, which causes testes to develop.
questions.explanation: Embryos with a Y chromosome (XY) develop testes due to SRY; without it (XX) ovaries develop. Fathers therefore determine the sex of offspring.

questions.prompt: Why is haemophilia much more common in males than in females?
options: The allele is dominant in males and recessive in females
The gene is on the Y chromosome
Males have only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele causes the disorder
Females produce extra factor VIII
questions.explanation: Haemophilia is X-linked recessive. Males (XY) have no second X to carry a dominant normal allele; females need two recessive alleles, which is rare.

questions.prompt: A carrier woman (X^H X^h) and a man without haemophilia (X^H Y) have a son. What is the probability that the son has haemophilia?
questions.explanation: A son always receives Y from his father and one of the mother's two X chromosomes, so he has a 1 in 2 chance of receiving X^h. Across all children the chance is 1 in 4.

questions.statement: In a pedigree, two unaffected parents having an affected child shows that the condition is caused by a recessive allele.
questions.explanation: The parents must both carry the allele without expressing it, so it must be recessive. A dominant condition would show in at least one parent.

questions.text: Human skin colour shows continuous variation because it is controlled by ___ genes plus environmental factors.
questions.explanation: Polygenic inheritance: many genes each add a small effect, and exposure to sunlight also affects pigmentation, giving a continuous range of phenotypes.

questions.prompt: In a box-and-whisker plot of student heights, what does the box represent?
options: The interquartile range, from the lower to the upper quartile, with the median inside
The mean plus and minus one standard deviation
The full range of heights
The 95% confidence interval
questions.explanation: The box spans the middle 50% of data (Q1 to Q3) with a line at the median. Whiskers extend towards the extremes; outliers may be shown separately.

questions.prompt: Order these from the least to the most variable phenotypic pattern.
items: One gene, two alleles, complete dominance
One gene, two alleles, incomplete dominance
One gene, multiple codominant and recessive alleles
questions.explanation: Complete dominance gives two phenotypes, incomplete dominance three, ABO-style multiple alleles four, and polygenic traits with environmental influence give continuous variation.

questions.prompt: Two plants heterozygous for two unlinked genes (AaBb x AaBb) are crossed. What phenotypic ratio is expected?
questions.explanation: Each parent makes four gamete types (AB, Ab, aB, ab) equally, giving 16 combinations: 9 dominant-dominant, 3 and 3 with one recessive trait, and 1 double recessive.

questions.text: A test cross of AaBb with aabb, with genes unlinked, is expected to give a ___ phenotypic ratio.
questions.explanation: The aabb parent only gives ab gametes, so offspring phenotypes directly reflect the four equally frequent gamete types of AaBb.

questions.statement: Independent assortment results from the random orientation of homologous pairs at metaphase I.
questions.explanation: Each bivalent lines up independently of the others, so alleles of genes on different chromosomes enter gametes in all combinations equally.

questions.prompt: In a dihybrid test cross, most offspring have parental phenotypes and a few have new combinations. What is the best explanation?
options: The genes are on different chromosomes
The genes are linked on the same chromosome, and crossing over produced a few recombinants
One allele is codominant
The parents were homozygous
questions.explanation: Linked genes tend to be inherited together, so parental combinations predominate. Crossing over between the loci in prophase I creates recombinant chromosomes and the minority recombinant offspring.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its meiotic cause.

pairs.right: Homologous chromosomes separate in anaphase I
Random orientation of bivalents in metaphase I

questions.explanation: Segregation separates the two alleles of each gene; independent assortment mixes unlinked genes; crossing over recombines linked genes.

questions.text: For a chi-squared test on a dihybrid cross with four phenotype classes, the degrees of freedom are ___.
questions.explanation: Degrees of freedom = number of categories − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3.

questions.prompt: A chi-squared value of 12.4 is calculated for a dihybrid cross (critical value at p = 0.05 with 3 degrees of freedom is 7.815). What should be concluded?
options: Accept the null hypothesis; results fit a 9:3:3:1 ratio
The test is invalid
The genes must be sex-linked
Reject the null hypothesis; the difference from the expected ratio is significant, possibly due to linkage
questions.explanation: The calculated value exceeds the critical value, so the difference between observed and expected is unlikely to be due to chance alone (p < 0.05). Gene linkage is a common reason.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a chi-squared test on cross data.
items: Calculate expected frequencies from the predicted ratio
Calculate the sum of (O − E)² / E
Find the critical value using degrees of freedom and p = 0.05
Compare the calculated and critical values to accept or reject the null hypothesis
questions.explanation: Expected values come from the Mendelian ratio and total offspring; the statistic is compared to the critical value at the right degrees of freedom.

questions.statement: Genes that are far apart on the same chromosome produce recombinants more frequently than genes close together.
questions.explanation: The further apart two loci are, the more likely a chiasma forms between them, so crossing over separates their alleles more often.

questions.prompt: What is the locus of a gene?
options: The specific position of the gene on a chromosome
The polypeptide coded for by the gene
The number of alleles of the gene
The base sequence of one allele
questions.explanation: Each gene has a fixed locus on a particular chromosome. Online databases record the loci of human genes and the polypeptides they code for.
